title: Tracebench: attention pipeline heapmap sweep and microtrace notes
content:
Purpose:
This doc contains the results from a targeted sweep using our tracebench harness that combines kernel-level traces (nsys), allocator heapmaps, and lightweight microbenchmarks to isolate attention-path hotspots. Goal: produce actionable tuning guidance for attention kernel selection (FlashAttention vs paged-attn vs fused ops) across latency-sensitive and throughput-focused workloads.

Executive summary:
- FlashAttention gives the best steady-state throughput on long sequences (>=512) for medium-to-large batches, but exhibits p50/p95 instability at small batch sizes due to underutilization and kernel launch serialization.
- Paged attention reduces peak memory pressure and L2 miss amplification for workloads with large cached KV histories (sequence growth across requests), but it increases kernel-count which hurts single-request latency unless kernel coalescing is applied.
- Fused ops (combined qkv+proj or attention+proj kernels) are the fastest for small-batch, low-seq (<256) latency targets because they eliminate inter-kernel memory traffic and reduce stream synchronization points.
- Heapmap traces show allocator fragmentation and cross-stream allocation spikes are correlated with rare 30–90ms tails; switching to a pooled arena for KV cache buffers eliminated these spikes in the controlled harness.

Environment and reproducibility:
- Hardware: NVIDIA A100 (40GB), CUDA 12.2, driver 535.xx.
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04
- Runtime build: serving-runtime@main (commit f2b9a3a), flashattention v1.3.2 (patched), paged-attn branch paged-prefetch-2025, fused-ops prototype PR#1987.
- Repro commands (example):
  - baseline trace: nsys profile --output trace_longseq --capture-range=kernel --trace=cuda,cublas,cudnn ./tracebench --model gpt-small --seq 1024 --batch 8 --profile-kernels
  - heapmap: TRACE_HEAPMAP=1 ./tracebench --seq 1024 --batch 8 --kv-history 512
  - micro-latency: ./tracebench --seq 64 --batch 1 --repeat 1000 --mode single_request
- NVTX annotations added to serving runtime around scheduler enqueue/dequeue, allocator alloc/free, and attention entry/exit to help correlate with nsys timelines.

Workloads and knobs swept:
- Sequence lengths: 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048
- Batch sizes: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16
- KV cache: disabled, small (128), medium (512), large (2048)
- Kernel variants: flashattention (default), paged-attn (page sizes 32/64/128), fused ops (qkv+attn fused, attn+proj fused)
- Scheduler: CUDA streams per request (1 vs pooled 4), concurrent streams limit (32, 64), coalescing window (0ms, 1ms, 5ms)
- Allocator: default cudaMalloc, pooled arena (jemalloc + CUDA IPC pools), pinned prepools for KV buffers

Instrumentation and metrics captured:
- Kernel timeline (nsys): kernel start/end, kernel name, stream id
- GPU metrics: SM utilization, achieved occupancy, warp efficiency, L2 traffic, DRAM throughput, tensor-core utilization
- Host-side: scheduler queue time, memcpy durations, allocator latencies, syscall stalls
- User-level metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, kernel count per request, memory-high-water mark, number of allocation calls per request

Key findings (detailed):
1) Small-batch latency tail due to kernel serialization + allocator stalls
- Observed long thin purple bands in nsys traces where many tiny kernels launch in sequence on the same stream with small gaps. These correlate with p95 spikes in single-request runs at batch=1, seq<=128 for FlashAttention builds.
- Root causes: (a) FlashAttention emits multiple kernels per attention pass for tiled reductions and softmax scaling which become launch overhead heavy at tiny workloads; (b) host-side allocator called per-request for temporary KV slices; occasional page faults/host allocations add 10–50ms.
- Mitigation validated: enable fused ops or increase coalescing window to group requests; switch to pooled KV arena eliminated allocator-related tails.

2) Paged attention tradeoffs
- Paged-attn reduces instantaneous GPU memory footprint by streaming pages for KV into a working set. In long-KV experiments (kv-history >=1024), L2 miss rate drops by 20–40% and DRAM bursts are smoother, improving throughput stability.
- Downsides: kernel count increases ~1.6x causing higher per-request kernel overhead. When batch=1 this increases p50 by ~5–8ms vs flashattention. With batch>=4 the paging overhead amortizes and paged-attn wins on peak throughput.
- Prefetching prefetch_depth=2 reduced page-miss stalls but increased bandwidth; tuned values depend on page size and sequence distribution.

3) Fused ops are best for low-latency small requests
- Fusing QKV+attn+proj reduced end-to-end device kernel count by up to 70% for small sequences and improved warp efficiency by ~10–15%. Net p50 improvement ~6–12ms for seq<=128 at batch=1.
- Maintain caution: fused kernels are larger; register pressure causes lower occupancy for very large model dims (d_model >=8192). We saw a drop in SM occupancy on A100 for a fused kernel compiled with default flags — needed register spilling tuning.

4) Heapmap and allocator observations
- Heapmap overlays show repeated allocation/free hotspots centered around the KV cache growth phases in chat-like traces. Fragmentation grows with mixed sequence workloads (alternating short and very long sequences).
- Switching to a per-stream pooled allocator (precreate 512 MB KV pools per-GPU) removed ~90% of host-side allocation events and reduced rare outlier latencies.

5) Scheduler and streams
- Using multiple CUDA streams and allowing the scheduler to overlap memcpy with compute reduced p99 for mixed workloads. However, naive multi-stream mapping increased contention on the allocator and L2 cache when many concurrent small requests targeted the same model shard.
- Best compromise: a small fixed pool of streams (4) combined with request coalescing window of 1ms gave consistent p95 improvements without adding allocator pressure.

Recommendations: short-term (next deployable changes)
- Default the runtime to: fused ops for small-model/low-latency tiers, FlashAttention for throughput tiers with seq>=512, and paged-attn enabled behind a config flag for very long-KV workloads.
- Implement a pooled KV arena per-GPU as a platform default to prevent host-side allocation tails.
- Add an adaptive coalescing limiter: dynamically increase coalescing when p95 > target and batch backlog low, otherwise pass-through.
- Expose two autotune knobs via console: attention_mode (fused|flash|paged) and coalesce_window_ms (0-5).

Recommendations: medium-term (engineering work)
- Work item: PR#1987 (fused ops) — resolve register pressure by generating two kernel variants tuned for low-dim and high-dim and auto-select at model-load time.
- Add kernel-side persistent-thread variants for small-batch low-latency path to reduce launch overhead (prototype shows ~2–3ms wins on seq<=128).
- Improve paged-attn prefetcher heuristics: adapt prefetch depth based on observed eviction rates and page fault history in the heapmap traces.

Open questions and experiments to run next:
- How does flashattention + fused-ops hybridization behave (flash internal kernels fused where possible)? Prototype attempt caused register ballooning; need autotuned tiling.
- Can we further reduce kernel counts by combining softmax+mul steps into single kernel for common sequence lengths? Quantify tradeoffs on occupancy.
- Evaluate performance on V100 and H100 to see how architecture differences shift the frontier.

Action items and owners:
- Ava: land pooled KV arena RFC and initial impl (JIRA-RT-4312).
- Diego: iterate on fused ops register allocation variants (GitHub PR 1987).
- Maya: add NVTX annotation coverage to scheduler and allocator; produce standard nsys capture template for infra team.
- Liam: run cross-arch sweep on H100 and document differences in a follow-up tracebench report.

Appendix: quick traces to inspect (how to read)
- Look for 'blue blocks' separated by thin gaps in nsys: these indicate kernel launch gaps; correlate with kernel name to see if multiple micro-kernels are used.
- Heapmap spike pattern: vertical red streaks aligned with NVTX 'alloc' markers indicate frequent host allocations; these are candidates for pooling.
- Kernel names: flash kernels often include 'flash' or 'fused_attn' prefixes; paged-attn shows 'page_copy' or 'page_stream' helper kernels.

Repro artifacts and links:
- Full sweep logs stored in s3://redwood-tracebench/2025-02-14-heapmap-sweep/ (internal)
- Example nsys capture: s3://redwood-tracebench/2025-02-14-heapmap-sweep/trace_longseq.qdrep
- Lightweight pipeline to reproduce micro-latency experiments: scripts/run_tracebench_sweeps.sh (repo: serving-runtime/scripts)

Notes and caveats:
- These experiments were run on single-GPU nodes; results will change for multi-GPU distributed serving (network comms and shard placement effects).
- Some fused-op variants used prototype kernels that are not yet hardened for integer overflow or unusual dtypes; test coverage in PR needed.

If you want, I can extract a short checklist for SRE/Release to experiment with a canary rollout of pooled arenas + fused ops for the ‘low-latency’ service tier.
